title: Shaping Integrity: Why Generative Artificial Intelligence Does Not Have to Undermine Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual and ethical question rather than testing an intervention: whether generative artificial intelligence (GAI) must undermine academic integrity in education, or whether it can be integrated in ways that support learning and ethical practice. The authors argue against the view that GAI is primarily a cheating tool and instead frame it as a potentially constructive educational resource when used responsibly. The discussion is grounded in ethical theory, constructivist learning theory, and self-determination theory.

The paper does not report an empirical study, trial, or quasi-experiment. Instead, it presents a position piece that synthesizes prior literature and offers illustrative examples of how GAI might be used in classrooms—for example, AI-supported writing feedback in language arts, simulations in history, lab assistants in science, and business-plan support. It also discusses the need to rethink assessment, promote digital literacy, and establish ethical guidelines and professional development for educators.

No specific participant sample is studied. The paper refers broadly to students, educators, and administrators across educational settings, with examples spanning high school classrooms and other educational domains, but these are hypothetical or literature-based illustrations rather than reported implementations. There is no direct evidence on K-12 foundational reading outcomes such as phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, oral reading fluency, vocabulary, or early reading comprehension.

The main conclusion is that GAI does not inherently erode academic integrity and can instead enhance motivation, engagement, digital literacy, and knowledge construction if implemented ethically and transparently. However, for the retrieval topic focused on causal evidence for foundational reading in K-12, this paper provides no direct causal evidence at all. Its relevance is adjacent and conceptual only: it discusses possible educational uses of generative AI, including language arts writing support, but does not evaluate reading interventions or report classroom outcome data.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a conceptual/theoretical discussion about ethical and pedagogical uses of generative AI in education, not an empirical study. It reports no randomized trial, quasi-experimental design, classroom causal identification strategy, sample, comparator, or quantitative outcome data.
impact_tier_rationale: Impact on student outcomes is unclear because the paper provides no direct intervention evidence or effect estimates. It is adjacent background literature rather than causal evidence on K-12 foundational reading outcomes.
